chunks: "The lost power doesn't disappear, it becomes heat.

Whatever the converter takes in and doesn't deliver is dissipated in the resistance of the FETs, inductor and traces, switching transitions, the core of the inductor, the controller's own bias current.
All of that ends up as thermal energy in the components, flows into the PCB and package, and out to the air. It's bad for several reasons.
First, temperature: the junction temperature rises by the loss times the thermal resistance, and every chip has a limit, often 125 to 150 degrees. A 1.
5 watt loss in a package with 40 degrees per watt is 60 degrees above ambient, so in a 70 degree enclosure you're at 130 and may hit thermal shutdown.
Second, reliability: failure rates roughly double every ten degrees or so, and electrolytic capacitor life drops similarly.
Third, performance drifts: FET resistance rises with temperature, so it gets worse as it heats up. Fourth, it's wasted energy, so battery runtime suffers.
And fifth, dealing with the heat costs area, heatsinks, fans and money.
So I'd design to the loss: compute it from efficiency, check the junction temperature at the worst-case ambient, and keep margin."
